stories.headline: Hockey women’s coach clears the air on his pre-World Cup absence
stories.deck: Hockey women’s coach clears the air on his pre-World Cup absence after team’s best-ever tournament showing in 52 years
stories.bodyText:
KOLKATA: It was 2020 and the pandemic had just begun.
Sjoerd Marijne, then the coach of the Indian women's hockey team, was in a cab en route to Bengaluru airport, from where he was supposed to fly back to the Netherlands to join his family. But midway through the ride, he changed his mind and returned to the city's Sports Authority of India centre.
It was a difficult decision, but Marijne chose to stay. A year later, he led India to a historic fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics.
Six years on, Marijne found himself making a very different choice. When he returned to take charge of the Indian women's team for a second stint, he once again had to find a way to combine his commitment to the team with being there for his family. This time, with the World Cup approaching, he chose to spend a few weeks with his family before rejoining the team - a decision that had been agreed upon when he took up the job.
But while Marijne was away from the team physically, he remained closely connected with its preparations. He followed every training session and practice match, stayed in touch with the players and conducted video meetings to ensure he remained on top of the process.
"I saw every training session and every practice match. I saw everything. So I wasn't there in person, but I was there," Marijne told TOI in an exclusive interview after India recorded their best World Cup finish in 52 years. "I had contact with the players and did video meetings with them, so I was on top of the process."
Marijne also credited his support staff, as well as the team's strength and conditioning staff, for giving him the confidence that the team was in good hands. "I had very good assistants like Matias Villa. Tim White, who is doing the under-21s, was also there. So, I knew they were in good hands," he said. "There's a lot of leadership in the team and they knew that they had to do well and give the example, so that's why this was possible."
When Marijne re-joined, he found the squad had continued along the same path. "It was all the same. For the girls, it also felt like I hadn't been away. So that is a positive thing," he said.
The Dutchman also stressed that while he was away physically, he had never stepped away from his responsibilities as coach. "It wasn't that for a few weeks I wasn't there mentally. I was only not physically there," he said.
For Marijne, the experience also highlighted the growing maturity within the group. The players were able to take responsibility, lean on the senior members and stay true to the team's structure and culture even with their coach away from the training ground.
"The players knew that I was overseeing everything," he said. "The main thing is that it looked like I was away. I was away physically, but for the players it didn't feel like I was away because I was still involved."
Perhaps that was the biggest reassurance for Marijne - that the team had developed enough trust and leadership to keep moving in the same direction, even when he wasn't physically there.

stories.headline: 'India took it for granted': Ex-cricketer on how Kohli could have changed result
stories.deck: According to Mohammad Kaif, India demonstrated a lack of intensity in their recent Test match in Colombo. He emphasized that the inclusion of Virat Kohli could have sharpened the team’s focus. With Sri Lanka managing to secure a draw, India’s prospects for World Test Championship qualification have become more complex, with seven matches ahead that could prove to be a steep challenge.
stories.bodyText:
Mohammad Kaif
 believes India missed the intensity and urgency needed to force a result in the Colombo Test, suggesting 
Virat Kohli
’s presence could have made a difference on a frustrating final day.
India were in a strong position to complete a 2-0 series sweep but could not finish the job after Sri Lanka resumed the final day with six wickets down. The visitors managed only two more dismissals, while Sonal Dinusha produced an unbeaten century to help the hosts secure a draw.
The result left India with a 1-0 series victory and made their road to the World Test Championship Final considerably tougher. India remain fifth in the WTC standings, with Sri Lanka sixth, and now have little room for error with seven Tests remaining.
India need to win at least six of those seven matches to keep control of their qualification hopes, with Australia also among their remaining opponents.
Kaif questions India’s intensity
Kaif felt the Colombo setback was partly down to India failing to maintain the kind of energy required during a long Test match.
The former India batter pointed towards 
Kohli
’s leadership style, particularly the way the former captain would constantly communicate with his teammates and keep the intensity high even during extended periods in the field.
“Playing Tests isn’t everyone’s cup of tea, boss. It’s a very long game and you have to keep bowling continuously. 
I felt that if someone like Virat Kohli had been playing this match, he would have been constantly shouting and keeping his team switched on," Kaif said.
According to Kaif, India appeared to believe that Sri Lanka’s resistance would eventually collapse because of the assistance available to the spinners, rather than actively creating pressure to force wickets.
“At times, I felt we took things for granted, thinking, ‘Just keep bowling, it will happen. The ball is turning so much, it will happen on its own," Kaif said.
‘Result would have been different’
Sri Lanka’s lower order and Dinusha’s resistance eventually frustrated India, with the batter remaining unbeaten on 133 and playing a crucial role in saving the Test.
Kaif argued that India needed to manufacture pressure rather than wait for opportunities to arrive. He also felt the team lacked the energy that Kohli traditionally brought to the field.
“We created very few things ourselves. Our energy levels were also very low. That is why I am saying, if Virat Kohli had been playing this Test, the result would have been different," Kaif said.
He suggested Kohli would have constantly pushed his teammates to stay aggressive and would have directly challenged Dinusha during his marathon resistance.
“The reason is that he would have been telling everyone, ‘Come on, Sarfaraz, come on, Jaiswal’ and he would have gone after Sonal as well. Who were we getting into confrontations with? We were getting into confrontations with Kumara," Kaif added.
The draw means India now face a demanding stretch in their WTC campaign, where further dropped opportunities could significantly hurt their chances of finishing among the top two.

stories.headline: Roger Federer heads to the Tennis Hall of Fame, says he ‘had the best time’ during his career
stories.deck: Roger Federer will have a chance to reflect back on it all on August 28 when he is enshrined in the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport
stories.bodyText:
Roger Federer loved to win, of course, and at the peak of his career almost always did.
All those victories and trophies he piled up alone would have made Federer remembered forever in tennis, but they were only part of the reason he enjoyed playing. He liked travelling to tournaments, meeting people and making new friends, whether they were on the other side of the net or sitting in the stands.
Only after he finished competing did Federer realize how much that impacted his legacy in the sport.
“I think when you retire, I think I said it before, that there was a lot of talk also about maybe my personality and what I brought to the game overall when I wasn't on court, which I was a little surprised,” Federer said. "I thought it was about, in the moment, forehands and backhands and saving break points and victories and all that stuff.
"But actually it becomes a little bit, not irrelevant eventually, but it's about what you were remembered for, how did you behave in the locker rooms or in the corridors or maybe with the media, or with the tournament directors, the ball kids." Federer will have a chance to reflect back on it all on Saturday (August 28, 2026) when he is enshrined in the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island.
The 45-year-old from Switzerland, who will be honored along with broadcaster and former player Mary Carillo, said it would be his first trip to Newport. That seemed surprising, given how many places he's gone for his tennis.
Sure, there was regular stops such as New York and London and Paris for Grand Slam tournaments, but there were also cities like Cape Town, South Africa, for an exhibition match against Rafael Nadal that drew nearly 52,000 fans; or Mexico City, for one against Alexander Zverev that drew more than 42,000.
Those were near the end of his career, when Federer was forced to limit his schedule for health reasons. He hated having to do so, because he liked going too many places, even ones that didn't host the biggest events.
“For me, if I look back, that's kind of what I'm very happy about, that I went through 25 years on tour, and actually felt like I made a lot of friends and a lot of people miss me,” Federer said.
"Same with fans. They come up to me and say, What a shame you're not playing anymore.' “Then I get a flashback saying it was an amazing time, and I say it every time. I loved it, and it's a shame I can't be on the tour anymore. But it was a great, great time and I miss it dearly.”
The fans clearly miss Federer. When he returned to the U.S. Open this week for an exhibition, his first time playing in Flushing Meadows since 2019, the lines of fans waiting to get into Arthur Ashe Stadium resembled a night in the second week of the tournament, not well before it even began.
Federer won five straight U.S. Open titles from 2004-08, during a stretch when he compiled a 247-15 record from 2004-06 and reached a record 10 consecutive Grand Slam finals from 2005-07, winning eight. He went on to win 1,251 matches and 103 tournaments, including 20 Grand Slams.
“He's the best I've ever played against,” Andre Agassi, Federer's opponent in the 2005 final, said in a video the U.S. Open showed before Federer took the court on Tuesday (August 25, 2026).
The way he won, with far more flair than some stuffy champions of the past but without the temper tantrums of others, earned him accolades that his skills alone couldn't. He won the ATP Tour's sportsmanship award every year from 2004-09, and again from 2011-17, and the fan favorite award every year from 2003-21. Those came while earning prize money of nearly $130.6 million.
Federer hits sometimes with his children — he and wife Mirka are parents of two sets of twins — and tries to attend a few events a year to keep him connected to the sport.
“I'm in a very comfortable place today, but I'm still happy to be out there and being in the tennis world from time to time, because it is the glue to everything that surrounds me still today,” Federer said.
“I had the best time, had a lot of friends on tour, from players to people who were organisers, et cetera. So I hope that a lot of the players who retire also feel the same way about the game, because I care dearly.”

stories.headline: Eng vs Pak 2nd Test: England in control at Lord’s and stretches lead to 261 after skittling Pakistan for 110
stories.deck: England's four seamers feasted on a Pakistan batting order that wasn't boosted by the return of captain Babar Azam
stories.bodyText:
England was bossing Pakistan by an imposing 261 runs after two days of the Lord's test on Friday (August 28, 2026).
The host side was 81-3 in its second innings when bad light stopped play and in total command after routing a depleted Pakistan for 110 in the afternoon.
Pakistan medium-pacers Khurram Shahzad and Mohammad Ali did well to prise out Ben Duckett, Jordan Cox and Joe Root in the last session but they were bowling in damage limitation mode.
Their batters' failure conceded an intimidating 180-run lead to England on the first innings. Pakistan hasn't totalled 180 in the series yet and was without opening batter Imam-ul-Haq, who suffered a left calf strain while fielding early Thursday (August 27, 2026) and won't reappear.
England won the first test in Leeds by an innings last week and may yet repeat the three-day feat and clinch the three-match series.
England's four seamers feasted on a Pakistan batting order that wasn't boosted by the return of captain Babar Azam.
Ollie Robinson took 4-11 from 13 overs, including six maidens. Jofra Archer had 3-26 from 11.2 and the fastest new-ball spell of his career, Josh Tongue claimed two wickets and Gus Atkinson was luckless.
“I could probably play until 40 at this rate (with this attack),” the 31-year-old Archer told broadcaster Sky Sports. “It's really nice having the extra seamers in the lineup. It's unbelievable when everybody is fit and firing. Each day it will be someone else's turn.”
Awais offers Pakistan's only resistance
Pakistan was blown away in 37.2 overs, and the bowlers were back in harness just over four hours after finishing England's first innings at 290 at noon.
The only resistance when Pakistan batted came from novice opener Azan Awais.
Embarrassingly out to the first ball of the series in Leeds, Awais dug in for 35 overs at Lord's. He debuted in May with a century in Bangladesh and was four runs shy of his third half-century. Awais faced 102 balls to score 46.
“I survived a good innings and built a little bit of my confidence,” Awais told the BBC.
His innings was remarkable considering the next best runs in Pakistan's scoreboard was 20 extras.
Awais was dropped on 8 off Atkinson and overturned being given out on 43. He was caught on the boundary after top-edging a pull at Robinson.
Robinson was heading toward a third player-of-the-match performance in three tests.
He came to the fore after lunch, pinning Saud Shakeel and Mohammed Rizwan to expose the tail. Robinson added Shahzad and Awais but couldn't grab another Lord's five-for.
Archer averaged 90.7 mph (146 kph) before lunch, topping at 95 mph (153 kph) but could nick off only Shan Masood, who moved up to open as Imam's replacement. Archer took out two tailenders at the end.
“I don't think the speed gun is accurate in this game, to be honest,” Archer said. “It didn't really feel that way. But I'll take it.” Tongue bagged Pakistan's most in-form batter, Abdullah Shafique, right on lunch. Shafique tried driving Tongue on 5 and was caught behind after England reviewed.
Tongue also got Babar straight after lunch. Coming back from a finger injury that made him miss the first test, Babar hit a couple of boundaries through the covers then edged Tongue to third slip on 8.
Tongue had a good day before he bowled. He earned a career-best batting score of 30 not out in the morning. Atkinson was last man out for 45.
They resumed England's first innings on 248-9 and their 10th-wicket partnership added a valuable 47 runs, 42 of them on Friday (August 28, 2026) to retake the momentum from Pakistan.
In their second bat, Duckett gave his wicket to Shahzad in the second over and Jordan Cox was pinned on the back pad by Shahzad in the fourth.
Root reviewed being dismissed by Ali on 24 but it was plumb, and he was out lbw for the ninth time in his last 12 test innings.
Still batting at stumps were the streaky but determined Emilio Gay on 30 and Harry Brook on 7.

briefs.headline: Praggnanandhaa’s golden summer: From Norway Chess glory to GCT crown
briefs.deck: R Praggnanandhaa clinched the prestigious Grand Chess Tour title in St Louis, USA, adding to his earlier triumph at the Norway Chess event this summer. As the first Indian to achieve such a notable feat, his exceptional mental fortitude was on display during the intense final rounds. This victory represents a significant milestone for Indian chess, especially ahead of the upcoming Olympiad.
briefs.bodyText:
Until this summer, no Indian had won the elite Norway Chess title. There was no Indian name alongside the Grand Chess Tour finale either. R Praggnanandhaa, that shy and super-sharp boy from Chennai, a Viswanathan Anand mentee like many from the city, now has both crowns to call his own.
Late on Thursday, Praggnanandhaa, the world No. 12, claimed the Grand Chess Tour (GCT) title, beating Fabiano Caruana 15-13 in St Louis, US, considered the new Linares in chess circles, and pocketed $200,000 in prize money. Praggnanandhaa thus became the first Indian and only the seventh player in the tournament’s 11-year history to achieve the feat.
It won’t be an exaggeration to call him the ‘unofficial’ Total Chess world champion ahead of the tournament’s inauguration next year and the pilot project later this year in Budapest.
The 21-year-old has chosen to play next month’s Olympiad over the lucrative Global Chess League in Bengaluru. That decision has worked out very well for him because he achieved a major success well in time for the Olympiad, where India will try to defend their maiden team gold medal in three weeks’ time.
The positive tidings for Indian chess don’t seem to end. The crop is fearless and the results are relentless, more importantly, at the ‘above Elo 2600’ level and not just below it or in the many online versions of the sport.
Earlier this year, Praggnanandhaa had done the unthinkable by beating world No. 1 Magnus Carlsen twice in classical games at Norway Chess, a feat that included an unprecedented sequence of four straight classical wins at the end of the tournament in Oslo.
If the Indian chess sun was shining brightly then, it has now just extended its rays to a new region.
Praggnanandhaa has shown year-round consistency by topping the GCT table, with only the top four making it to the finale. And then, despite losing the first classical game of the final to Caruana in the title clash and messing up a probable equaliser in the second classical game, worth six points, he still displayed admirable mental strength.
Praggnanandhaa won both rapid games, worth four points each, to take the lead over the highly regarded Caruana before drawing the four-game blitz section 4-4, with one win for either player. He had beaten German super talent Vincent Keymer in the semifinals.
While this may be subjective, and the chess world has its favourites, experts consider Praggnanandhaa a more well-rounded Indian player than world champion Gukesh and former Elo 2800 member Arjun Erigaisi, partly due to his technical prowess and more universal style of play.
That is why his failed campaigns at the 2024 and 2026 Candidates, and the manner in which he imploded, were particularly disheartening for Indian fans.
Praggnanandhaa’s St Louis schedule was gruelling. He played 27 rapid and blitz games, then nine classical games, and another 16 games in the semifinals and finals of the Tour.
Now, he can rest with a sense of achievement, a high like no other.
When his sister Vaishali was not doing too well at the Classical Cairns Cup for women, being played concurrently at the same venue, Praggnanandhaa was plotting his own grand prize. The roles were reversed at the Cyprus Candidates earlier this year when Vaishali won the women’s title and Praggnanandhaa finished seventh in the eight-player field.
Not that Praggnanandhaa hadn’t proved himself before at the elite level. He burst into the limelight by reaching the 2023 World Cup final in Baku, the birthplace of the great Garry Kasparov, in Azerbaijan, and has now stamped his authority on the GCT Tour, which has been the brainchild of the Russian.
In between his knockout World Cup run and the Norway title, he had several high points. But those came largely in the classical section, with triumphs at Wijk aan Zee, the GCT Romania leg and the UzChess Cup in 2025, all in classical chess.
World championship challenger Javokhir Sindarov had humbled Praggnanandhaa twice at the Cyprus Candidates. The Indian avenged those defeats at the Sinquefield Cup, where he finished joint first.
Keymer defeated Praggnanandhaa at Sinquefield before getting knocked out by the Indian’s cerebral powers in the semifinals of the Tour Finale.

briefs.headline: 'He keeps faking injuries': Ex-Paki chief selector's allegation against Imam
briefs.deck: Former chief selector Mohammad Wasim has claimed that Imam-ul-Haq has a history of faking injuries. During the recent Lord's Test match, Imam-ul-Haq sustained a calf injury that scans later confirmed to be a low-grade strain, sidelining him from the game. Meanwhile, Pakistan continues to face challenges in the ongoing Test series as England's pace bowlers exerted authority over Pakistan's batting…
briefs.bodyText:
Pakistan
 opener Imam-ul-Haq’s calf injury has come under fresh scrutiny after former chief selector Mohammad Wasim made a startling claim about the batter’s history of allegedly faking injuries.
Imam was ruled out of the remainder of the Lord’s Test against England after suffering a left calf strain while fielding on the opening day. However, Wasim has now alleged that the batter had previously used injury concerns to avoid playing, and claimed he was warned about one such incident before it happened.
Speaking about Imam’s alleged injury history, Wasim said:
"In 2022 Multan test, the physio warned me in advance that he is going to fake an injury soon. And he did that."
Wasim’s remarks have added another layer to the controversy surrounding Imam, who missed Pakistan’s ongoing second Test against England after the Pakistan Cricket Board confirmed that scans showed a low-grade calf strain.
What happened at Lord’s?
Imam picked up the injury during the opening day of the Lord’s Test and spent time away from the field during Thursday’s evening session.
The PCB subsequently confirmed the nature of the injury.
"Scans later confirmed a low-grade calf strain and Imam is currently receiving treatment under the supervision of the Pakistan medical team," the PCB said.
"His participation in the remainder of the Test depends on treatment leading to recovery," it added.
Imam had opened the innings alongside young Azan Awais during the first Test at Leeds, which Pakistan lost by an innings inside three days.
He was subsequently unable to take part in the remainder of the Lord’s Test, leaving Pakistan without one of their established opening batters.
Pakistan struggle continues
Pakistan’s problems at Lord’s extended well beyond Imam’s absence.
England took a commanding position after bowling Pakistan out for just 110, securing a first-innings advantage of 180 runs. The visitors had yet to reach 180 in an innings during the series.
England’s pace attack made the most of the conditions, with Ollie Robinson producing figures of 4-11 from 13 overs, including six maidens. Jofra Archer claimed 3-26 from 11.2 overs, while Josh Tongue took two wickets and Gus Atkinson went wicketless.
Pakistan were dismissed in only 37.2 overs, having returned to bat less than a few hours after England had been bowled out for 290.
By the end of the second day, England had stretched their overall lead to 261 runs after reaching 81-3 in their second innings before bad light brought an early close.
Khurram Shahzad and Mohammad Ali did manage to remove Ben Duckett, Jordan Cox and Joe Root in the final session, but England remained firmly in control.
Wasim’s allegation now puts the spotlight on Imam’s injury record, although the PCB has officially diagnosed his latest setback as a low-grade calf strain.

briefs.headline: ‘India messed up big time’: Ex-captain sounds alarm after costly Colombo blunder
briefs.deck: India's ambitions for World Test Championship qualification took a blow following a drawn Test match in Colombo. This result denied them a chance to sweep the series against Sri Lanka. Cricketer Krishnamachari Srikkanth expressed concerns about the implications for the team's future. With only seven matches left, India must secure victories in at least six to stay in contention for the title.
briefs.bodyText:
India’s World Test Championship hopes have taken a hit after the Colombo Test ended in a draw, with former India cricketer Krishnamachari Srikkanth warning that the missed opportunity could have serious consequences for their qualification campaign.
India appeared well placed to complete a 2-0 series sweep after taking control of the second Test. Sri Lanka began the final day with six wickets down, leaving India needing only four more wickets to seal victory.
Instead, the visitors could manage just two wickets as Sonal Dinusha produced a stunning unbeaten century to frustrate India. The Sri Lankan batter remained unbeaten on 133 and stitched together vital partnerships with the lower order, helping the hosts survive and force a draw after following on.
The result meant India had to settle for a 1-0 series victory rather than the 2-0 sweep that had looked within reach.
The dropped opportunity in Colombo could prove significant in the race for the WTC Final. India remain fifth in the standings, with Sri Lanka sixth, and now have very little room for error across their remaining seven Tests.
According to Srikkanth, India may need an almost perfect run from here to stay in control of their qualification hopes.
"This draw will make it difficult for India to qualify for the WTC final. Even if India wins five or six of the last seven matches, they'll have to depend on other results. It's questionable if India can beat Australia 5-0 at home. If we give rank turners in that series, Australia can also beat India," Srikkanth said on his YouTube channel.
India have seven Tests left in their WTC campaign and need to win at least six of them to control their own destiny.
A major challenge will come when Australia travel to India. Srikkanth cautioned against assuming that home conditions will guarantee results, particularly if India prepare heavily turning pitches.
Srikkanth was particularly critical of India’s failure to close out the Colombo Test after creating a strong position.
He also highlighted Dinusha’s contribution, with the Sri Lankan batter producing twin centuries at the Sinhalese Sports Club and playing a decisive role in keeping his team alive on the final day.
"India messed up big time. Sonal Dinusha was amazing throughout the series. This is where you miss a bowler like Bumrah. You need a finishing bowler like him. Though rain helped Sri Lanka a bit, India should have won the match hands down," said Srikkanth.
Dinusha’s unbeaten 133 proved crucial as Sri Lanka survived India’s late push and secured a draw, leaving the visitors with a 1-0 series win but also a potentially costly setback in their WTC campaign.

briefs.headline: Why Aug 29 Matters? National Sports Day honours Dhyan Chand; story of the Wizard
briefs.deck: On August 29, National Sports Day commemorates Major Dhyan Chand, the iconic figure in Indian hockey whose brilliance led to three Olympic gold medals. This day not only celebrates his legacy, but also promotes the spirit of sportsmanship, fitness, and healthy living among the youth, as well as acknowledging the accolades of India's sports heroes, fueling inspiration for future generations.
briefs.bodyText:
He scored more than 400 goals, inspired India’s dominance of world hockey and was the central figure in the country’s first hat-trick of Olympic gold medals. Decades after his playing career ended, Major Dhyan Chand remains one of the most revered figures in Indian sporting history.
His contribution is remembered every year on August 29, his birth anniversary, which is celebrated across India as 
National Sports Day
.
The day, established in 2012, is a tribute to the hockey great popularly known as the ‘Hockey Wizard’ and ‘The Magician’. It also serves as a reminder of the importance of sports, physical activity and fitness, while providing an occasion to celebrate the achievements of India’s leading sportspersons.
But why was Dhyan Chand chosen as the inspiration behind National Sports Day, and who was the man whose extraordinary hockey career helped put India at the top of the sporting world?
Why is National Sports Day celebrated on August 29?
National Sports Day is observed on August 29 because it marks the birth anniversary of Dhyan Chand, who was born in Allahabad, now Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, in 1905.
The annual observance was established in 2012 to honour his contribution to Indian hockey and to highlight the broader importance of sports and fitness in everyday life.
The occasion has traditionally also been associated with the presentation of India’s major sporting honours. Over the years, the country’s top sports awards have been presented by the President of India at a ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan around National Sports Day.
The country’s highest sporting honour, the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award, also carries the hockey legend’s name. The award was previously known as the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna before being renamed.
National Sports Day is also marked by sporting and fitness activities at schools, colleges and other institutions across the country. The idea is to encourage young people to participate in sports and understand the importance of maintaining an active and healthy lifestyle.
The government’s Khelo India programme, which began in its present form in 2017-18, has become one of its major initiatives aimed at promoting sports among different age groups.
In 2019, Prime Minister 
Narendra Modi
 launched the Fit India Movement on National Sports Day, further strengthening the focus on physical fitness and active lifestyles.
File Pic: Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium in New Delhi. (PTI Photo)
Who was Major Dhyan Chand?
Dhyan Chand was born Dhyan Singh on August 29, 1905. He later became one of the defining figures of Indian hockey during the sport’s golden era.
His international career stretched from 1926 to 1948, and he represented India in 185 matches, scoring more than 400 goals according to the figures traditionally associated with his career.
His journey into hockey, however, was not immediate. As a youngster, his initial interest was reportedly in wrestling. He took up hockey at around the age of 14 and eventually joined the British Indian Army, where his extraordinary talent began to emerge.
His dedication to the sport became legendary. With much of his day occupied by regimental duties, he would practise hockey at night under the moonlight. The story is widely associated with how he came to be known as Dhyan Chand, with ‘Chand’ meaning moon in Hindi.
His rise was rapid. After impressing in Army competitions, he earned his place in the Indian team for the 1928 Olympic Games in Amsterdam.
There was little indication that his international career would eventually become synonymous with Indian hockey’s greatest period of dominance.
Dhyan Chand and India’s Olympic gold hat-trick
Dhyan Chand was a key figure as India won three successive Olympic gold medals in hockey at the 1928, 1932 and 1936 Games.
At the 1928 Olympics, he scored two goals in India’s 3-2 victory over the Netherlands in the final and finished as the tournament’s leading scorer with 14 goals.
His extraordinary scoring continued at the 1932 Games in Los Angeles, where India successfully defended its Olympic title.
But it was at the 1936 Berlin Olympics that one of the most famous chapters of his career unfolded.
India defeated Germany 8-1 in the final to complete a third consecutive Olympic hockey triumph. Dhyan Chand played a starring role, scoring two goals in the final. A famous account of the match says he played barefoot during the second half, although the detail has become part of the mythology surrounding his career.
For India, Dhyan Chand and the hockey team provided one of the defining sporting performances of the Games.
Dhyan Chand
The hockey wizard who scored more than 400 goals
Dhyan Chand’s reputation was built not merely on his goal tally but on the extraordinary control and skill he displayed with the hockey stick.
His stick work, passing ability, positioning and understanding of the game earned him the enduring descriptions of ‘Hockey Wizard’ and ‘The Magician’.
His career continued until 1948, when he was 42 years old. By then, he had become one of the most celebrated hockey players in the world.
There are several famous stories surrounding his ability. One oft-repeated tale claims that officials at a match had his stick inspected because they suspected there was something unusual about it after watching his extraordinary control of the ball.
Whether anecdotal or embellished over the years, such stories reflect the almost mythical status Dhyan Chand acquired during his career.
His influence extended beyond his own achievements. His success helped establish India as a dominant force in international hockey during the pre-Independence era and inspired generations of players.
Why Dhyan Chand remains relevant on National Sports Day
Dhyan Chand’s legacy goes beyond his three Olympic gold medals and remarkable scoring record.
His career is remembered as an example of discipline, dedication, skill and commitment to sport — qualities that National Sports Day seeks to promote among young Indians.
He was also recognised by the Indian government for his contribution to hockey. In 1956, he was awarded the Padma Bhushan, the country's third-highest civilian honour at the time.
Dhyan Chand retired from the Army as a Major in the Punjab Regiment in 1956. He continued to be associated with hockey after his playing career, including through coaching and mentoring.
His birth anniversary therefore became an appropriate occasion for India to celebrate not only one of its greatest sporting icons but the wider role of sport in society.
August 29: Celebrating sport beyond Dhyan Chand
National Sports Day today has a much broader significance than remembering one hockey player.
It is an opportunity to recognise athletes who have brought glory to India, encourage children to take up sport and promote physical fitness across society.
From schools and colleges organising competitions and fitness activities to the recognition of outstanding sportspersons, August 29 has become a day when India turns its attention to the value of sporting excellence.
Yet at the heart of the occasion remains the story of a young man named Dhyan Singh, who practised hockey under the moon after completing his military duties and went on to become one of the greatest players the sport has ever produced.
Nearly half a century after his death, his name continues to define India’s National Sports Day — a fitting tribute to the man who helped make Indian hockey synonymous with Olympic greatness.

briefs.headline: PCB’s Lord’s Test threat exposed? Sarfaraz Ahmed breaks silence amid controversy
briefs.deck: Pakistan's head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed stated players were unaware of a reported PCB threat. This controversy emerged during the lunch break on the first day. The interview featured Imran Khan's sons discussing their father's situation. Pakistan's players returned to the field after lunch and the Test continued. England ended the second day in a strong position.
briefs.bodyText:
Pakistan
 head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed has said he and his players were completely unaware of the Pakistan Cricket Board’s reported threat to withdraw from the Lord’s Test after Sky Sports aired an interview with 
Imran Khan
’s sons.
The controversy emerged during the lunch break on the first day of the second Test between England and Pakistan, with reports claiming the PCB had warned the England and Wales Cricket Board that Pakistan could abandon the match and potentially pull out of the remainder of the three-Test tour if the interview was broadcast.
However, Pakistan’s players returned to the field after lunch and the Test continued as scheduled.
Asked about the incident after the end of play on Day 2, Sarfaraz said the reported developments had not reached the dressing room and insisted his attention remained on the match.
"I don't know anything. I'm just focusing on the match. You're talking about the interview? We don't know about the interview," Sarfaraz told reporters.
The Pakistan coach was then asked whether there had been any possibility of the players refusing to return for the second session on the opening day.
"All are OK. We were having lunch at that time," he replied.
Interview involving Imran Khan’s sons
The interview in question featured Suleiman and Kasim Khan, the sons of former Pakistan captain and prime minister Imran Khan, and was conducted by former England captain and Sky Sports broadcaster Michael Atherton.
During the conversation, the two brothers spoke about their father’s treatment and security while he remains in custody. They also questioned the UK government’s response to his situation.
A version of the interview was ultimately broadcast, despite the reported concerns raised by the PCB.
In Pakistan, however, viewers did not see the interview. The Test is being shown by state broadcaster PTV using Sky’s international feed, but PTV did not air the segment involving Imran Khan’s sons.
Political backdrop
The episode has unfolded against a politically sensitive backdrop, with PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi also serving as Pakistan’s interior minister.
Imran Khan, 73, remains one of the most prominent figures in Pakistan’s cricket and political history. He spent 21 years as an international cricketer and led Pakistan to their first World Cup triumph in 1992.
He later entered politics and served as Pakistan’s prime minister from 2018 to 2022. Khan has been in prison since 2023 after being convicted in corruption-related cases, charges he has denied.
Despite the reported threat surrounding the Sky Sports interview, Pakistan’s participation in the Lord’s Test was not disrupted.
England ended the second day in a strong position, moving 261 runs ahead after reaching 81 for 3 in their second innings.

briefs.headline: Hockey India announces ₹50 lakh cash award for women's hockey team on historic 5th place finish at World Cup
briefs.deck: The team went through the campaign with just one defeat, holding higher-ranked sides China, England and Australia to draws and recording a 6-1 win over South Africa, before completing their run under Chief Coach Sjoerd Marijne with the win over Germany
briefs.bodyText:
Hockey India on Friday (August 28, 2026) announced a cash award of ₹50 lakh for the Indian women's team in recognition of their historic fifth-place finish at the FIH Hockey World Cup.
Salima Tete's side sealed the milestone with a 3-1 win over World No. 5 Germany in the 5th/6th place classification match in Amstelveen on Thursday (August 27, 2026), marking India's best result at the tournament since they finished fourth at the inaugural edition in 1974.
The team went through the campaign with just one defeat, holding higher-ranked sides China, England and Australia to draws and recording a 6-1 win over South Africa, before completing their run under Chief Coach Sjoerd Marijne with the win over Germany.
Congratulating the team on the achievement, Hockey India President Dilip Tirkey said, "This is a historic result for Indian women's hockey. To finish fifth at a World Cup after 52 years is a testament to the hard work, resilience and fighting spirit this team has shown throughout the tournament."
"On behalf of Hockey India, I am pleased to announce a cash award of ₹50 lakh for the team as a token of our appreciation, and I hope this inspires the players to keep raising the bar," he added.

briefs.headline: Total World Chess Championship Tour muscles its way into global calendar
briefs.deck: Its pilot will be held at Budapest from November 10 to 21 with many of the biggest names in chess, including World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen, participating
briefs.bodyText:
The chess calendar is crowded. Top players rarely get to take a breather these days with so many big events, across formats, taking place across the globe.
And it is going to get even more crowded with the newly launched Total World Chess Championship Tour. Its pilot will be held at Budapest from November 10 to 21. Lined up for the event are many of the biggest names in chess, headlined by World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen.
There are three Indians in the fray — Arjun Erigaisi and the Chennai siblings R. Praggnanandhaa and R. Vaishali. Arjun is one of the eight top 10 players that will compete in Budapest.
The presence of men like Fabiano Caruanan (World No. 2), Vincent Keymer (No. 5) and Wesley So (No. 6) ensures it would be a stiffly contested event, which will feature 24 players in all.
The first full tour will begin next year with four legs to be played in cities across the world. Conceived by Norway Chess, with blessings from the world chess governing body FIDE, the new tour combines different formats of chess — classical, rapid and blitz.
There are, of course, separate World championships for all those categories, and the classical format Total World Chess Championship is not quite classical in fact: the time control is 45 minutes with an increment of 30 seconds per move.
That may look more rapid than classical, for which the time control is usually 90 minutes for the first 40 moves and then 30 minutes for the rest of the game with increment.
Total Chess, to be fair, isn’t calling its format classical, but fast classical. That makes sense. For, classical chess needs to retain its prime place.
It is still the World champions in classical chess — be it Bobby Fischer, Garry Kasparov or Viswanathan Anand — that the world will always remember vividly.
The Total Chess Championship Tour, though, is a welcome addition to the mind sport. The more the merrier.
